title: By cutting data layers, researchers create fast, explainable landslide detection AI
excerpt: Publishing original research in a top-tier academic journal has been an ambition of Arsalaan Ahmad's since he enrolled in an undergraduate computer science program at Cardiff University.
content_html:
Publishing original research in a top-tier academic journal has been an ambition of Arsalaan Ahmad's since he enrolled in an undergraduate computer science program at Cardiff University.

Among the self-confessed space nerd's achievements are teaching himself machine learning and amassing 50 million visits for a Roblox game he developed.

Now, having recently graduated from the School of Computer Science and Informatics, Ahmad is reflecting on becoming the lead author of a research paper in Frontiers in Remote Sensing.

"The first thing I did was print the paper out so I could keep it in my room alongside the poster I had made about our findings," said Ahmad, who earned a BSc in computer science.

The 23-year-old was born and raised in Oman, where the geography inspired the idea behind the research paper.

"I developed a real interest in landslides living among the mountains," Ahmad recalled.

"In Oman, authorities take extensive measures during road and settlement construction to prevent natural disasters, which are increasing because of the effects of climate change."

A 'black box problem'

The paper, co-authored by Ahmad's mentors Dr. Oktay Karakuş and Professor Paul Rosin, examines the use of satellite AI to map natural disasters such as landslides.

The team explored a "black box problem" in which current AI models are bloated by up to 30 layers of data, making them slow, expensive and impossible to audit.

Instead, they developed a framework that strips away redundant data to create a compact, 8-channel AI model that matches the accuracy of massive systems but runs significantly faster.

This allows life-saving disaster AI to run on cheaper hardware, the researchers say. Their solution also runs in resource-constrained environments, delivering fast, explainable maps to emergency teams when every second counts.

The opportunity to make his idea a reality came when Ahmad applied for an on-campus internship.

"I reached out to a few professors about the idea to work on something related to landslide segmentation, but most of them were pretty skeptical," he said.

"Professor Paul Rosin, who was our module leader for Computational Math, thought the idea was interesting, and he encouraged me to write an internship proposal.

"I took a lot of time over it, researching different angles we could approach, and met with Paul to see what might work best. Eventually, the proposal was accepted, and I got to take full ownership of the project from beginning to end."

Rosin, a professor of computer vision at Cardiff University's School of Computer Science and Informatics and one of the paper's co-authors, said, "The ideal outcome of our on-campus internships is to create something which might be publishable but, in my experience, it is rarely achieved. Of course, some work was required to create and revise a technical description of Arsalaan's work to a level suitable for publication. But he did it.

"Overall, I am very pleased with the outcome. There are many challenges to overcome, such as learning a large amount of new information in a short time, learning new research and writing-for-publication skills, as well as coping with the demands of his regular course workload.

"Given that Arsalaan rose to this challenge, I expect he will continue to succeed in the future. I wish him the best of luck."

'An on-campus internship gave me the environment to start'

"The response has been overwhelming," Ahmad said.

"I've had a lot of praise over the fact that I published a first-author paper as an undergraduate. I understand this isn't common, but I'd encourage others to do the same. Don't wait for a Ph.D. or try to solve massive, saturated problems. Pick a narrow, specific bottleneck where you can apply skills you already have.

"Most importantly, be proactive about reaching out. Professors and research groups are actively looking for students who can build and execute. An on-campus internship gave me the environment to start, but the work happens when you treat research as practical problem-solving.

"It's also really important not to be discouraged when your original idea doesn't work out. Research is all about trying things from different angles. Don't be afraid to ask for guidance, pivot here and there, and you'll eventually land on something worthy of writing about."

With an academic paper already under his belt and ambitions for another, postgraduate study and research might seem like the obvious destination for Ahmad.

"It's just the start. I believe I can do a lot more; I'm just 23 after all," Ahmad said.

"I have thought about a Ph.D., and I love publishing papers, but right now, I'm thinking of taking my skills into the vast startup market in the U.K."

Ahmad was recently accepted into the fall 2026 cohort of Entrepreneurs First, an international business incubator and venture capital firm that supports individuals in building technology companies.

Selected among the top 2% of candidates from a competitive international applicant pool of more than 3,000, he plans to use the opportunity to pursue his own startup in energy and climate technology.

"I want to take direct ownership of translating remote sensing and computer vision research into deployed commercial products before considering a Ph.D. down the line," he said.

"Building for the real world right now is where the biggest impact lies."
